How do you get a wildcard mask from a subnet mask?
216.0.5.2/30: network, broadcast, and the other usable address?
Network 216.0.5.0, broadcast 216.0.5.3. The other usable address is 216.0.5.1.

/20 blocks go in 16s in the third octet: 0, 16, 32, 48...
Network 10.1.32.0, broadcast 10.1.47.255.

/30: 2
/29: 6
/27: 30
/24: 254
(2 to the power of the host bits, minus network and broadcast.)
Are 10.0.0.1/30 and 10.0.0.5/30 in the same subnet?
No. .1 is in 10.0.0.0/30 (0-3); .5 is in 10.0.0.4/30 (4-7). Two routers addressed like this won't talk.
Are 192.168.1.62/26 and 192.168.1.65/26 in the same subnet?
ip address 10.10.0.0 255.255.255.0 returns '% Bad mask /24 for address 10.10.0.0'. What's wrong?
The address, not the mask. With /24, 10.10.0.0 is the network address, which can't go on an interface. Use a host address like 10.10.0.1.
Can you put 10.10.0.255 255.255.254.0 on an interface?
Yes. /23 spans 10.10.0.0-10.10.1.255, so 10.10.0.255 is an ordinary host address. It only looks like a broadcast.
Can you put 192.168.5.63 255.255.255.192 on an interface?
No. With /26, .63 is the broadcast address of 192.168.5.0/26.
Gi0/0 has 10.1.1.1/24. You configure 10.1.1.200/24 on Gi0/1. What happens?
Rejected: '% 10.1.1.0 overlaps with GigabitEthernet0/0'. A router won't put two interfaces in the same subnet.

Why do point-to-point links between routers usually use /30?
It has exactly two usable addresses, one for each end, and wastes nothing else.
What are the private IPv4 ranges?

172.32.10.5: no, it's public. The private block stops at 172.31.255.255.
172.31.200.1: yes.
Does an address's class (A/B/C) matter to modern routing?

No. Routing is classless: only the mask matters. Classes still show up in IOS output (the 'variably subnetted' header) and as the default size when a routing protocol network statement has no wildcard.
